summary: IR, not shadow, sets the limit. Exact point-source integration (verified against both shell closed forms to 1e-4) gives, per 1 % coverage, 4.16 W/m2 of absorbed IR from a uniform 0.91 AU shell (42 % from far-side fronts seen through the gaps), offset by 2.38 of self-dimming: net +1.5-1.8 per 1 %, and +41-45 W/m2 at the 22 % ceiling (279-283 W/m2 absorbed: at the runaway threshold). Per sail the forcing is alpha_E J r^2 |cos gamma|/d^2 and r^2 cancels, so only distance to Earth and face angle matter: hot inner shells and polar rings change IR by <= 30 %, a keep-out cap halves IR but loses the dimming, exterior shells fall as 1/r^2 but cost r^2 in mass (3/5/10 AU: 2.1/0.8/0.2 % coverage from the whole fleet). Best: a far-side co-orbital cloud (a = 0.9987 AU, L3 +-90 deg, |lat| <= 30 deg): no shadow, held with ~1e-8 m/s2 (1/2500 of the authority), uncontrolled sails librate no closer than 0.29 AU. Earth always lies in its sails' sunward hemisphere, so an IR-dark low-e front (eps 0.05-0.10, chiplets 105-110 C, -16-19 % FLOP/J) cuts IR to 0.15-0.29 W/m2 per 1 % (1.43 as designed, 0.85 at 85 C); +35-46 % mass per W. An L1 thermostat of ordinary sails (0.42 % of sunlight per W/m2, ~1e-10 of the swarm) cancels the global mean, but each W/m2 cancelled costs -0.76 % precipitation, +0.23 W/m2 at the poles, +0.27 K stratosphere. With cancelled IR <= 2.5 X: X = 1 W/m2 allows f = 14 % (5.6e+39 FLOP/s, 50 % of the 1.1e40 ceiling; 13 % at 85 C); X = 0.1: 1.6 % (6 %); X = 4: 19 % (68 %). Passive (no thermostat), 1 W/m2 allows 6.2 % (shell 0.68 %). Fine dust must stay < 1e-7-3e-6 of the 3e19 kg/yr loss stream. The cloud glows at 1.7-4.8 cd/m2 per 1 % within 45 deg of the Sun (0.3 lux per 1 % after twilight): holding that under full-moon level caps f at ~0.8 % (2.4 % with a rho_v 0.001 front), so visible light, not heat, may bind first.

ir_model.method: Point-source sum over sails on a sphere of radius r (grid of 1.15e6 cells centred on Earth's direction, refined near it): each face is Lambertian with radiosity J (front: eps_f sigma T^4 / (1 - g(1 - eps_f)) incl. front-to-front exchange, g = f; back: eps_b sigma T^4); Earth (alpha_IR 0.95) absorbs alpha_E J A cos(gamma) / (4 pi d^2) per sail as an Earth-surface average; front rays that cross the sphere again are blocked with probability tau(exit); rays grazing the Sun are blocked. Sub-bandgap reflection (1 - alpha = 0.20 of sunlight, 2100+ film) is either diffuse (Lambertian front) or specular (retro-reflected toward the Sun in a 2.9 deg cone: film slope 1.3 deg + pointing + solar disk) and absorbed by Earth at 0.70. Film T from the model.js radiosity formula with 2100+ optics (alpha 0.80, eps 0.86/0.93). Scripts: irlib.py, ir_model.py.

closed_forms.per_sail: Earth-average absorbed = alpha_E J A |cos gamma| / (4 pi d^2); with J ~ alpha S0 / (r^2 (eps_f + eps_b)) the r^2 cancels: F/f = alpha_E alpha S0 [eps_face/(eps_f+eps_b)] |cos gamma| / d^2 (d in AU). Only the distance to Earth and the face angle matter, not the distance to the Sun.
closed_forms.interior_shell: F = alpha_E f alpha_eff S0 / 4 x 2/(1 + cos theta_s), sin theta_s = r (energy conservation + uniform disk of radiance (f J_b + (1-f) f J_f)/pi); dimming f x 238 W/m2.
closed_forms.exterior_shell: F = alpha_E f J_f, J_f = eps_f sigma T^4/(1 - f(1 - eps_f)) (Earth inside an isotropic cavity field).
closed_forms.coorbital_1AU: cos(gamma)/d^2 = 1/(4 sin(psi/2)) for a sail at heliocentric angle psi from Earth on the 1 AU circle: 0.25 at L3, 0.29 at 120 deg, 0.35 at 90 deg, 0.50 at 60 deg; far-hemisphere solid-angle mean 0.293.

ceiling_check.vs_skeptic: skeptic +49 W/m2 (287 absorbed) assumed all intercepted light re-emitted as IR absorbed at 0.95; with alpha 0.80 the 20 % NIR is absorbed like sunlight (0.70): +41 to +45 W/m2, 279-283 W/m2 absorbed - at the runaway threshold rather than 5 W/m2 beyond it. Conclusion unchanged.

anisotropy_findings: Interior shells: IR per coverage is set by energy conservation; only the sphere factor 2/(1+cos theta_s) depends on r: 2.65 (0.3 AU) vs 3.66 (0.91 AU) W/m2 per 1 %. Self-dimming (-2.38) is the same, so net per coverage falls from 1.77 to 0.68.

Time-averaged rings (r < 1, synodic drift): polar ring 0.83x the uniform IR at 0.91 AU (0.85x at 0.3 AU); i = 60 deg 0.88x; ecliptic ring 4.8x (it passes 0.09 AU from Earth) plus 23x the dimming. Inclination buys <= 17 %.
Polar caps (|lat| > 30-60 deg) would give 0.48-0.65x, but Keplerian orbits cross the ecliptic: not realisable without g_sun-scale thrust (1e2x the sail authority).

A co-moving keep-out cap of 24.5 deg at 0.91 AU (no back faces visible) cuts IR 3.66 -> 1.85 W/m2 per 1 % but also removes the self-dimming: passive net 1.77 -> 2.34. Wider caps barely help (1.46 at 120 deg): the far-side front faces seen through the gaps remain.

Co-orbital at 1 AU (fixed in Earth's frame): front faces face Earth across the Sun; per 1 %: 1.24 at L3 only, 1.43 for L3+-90/|lat|<=30, 1.47 for the whole far hemisphere, 2.6 at the L4/L5 points. Far-side placement is 2.7x better than the 0.85-0.92 AU shell IR, not 10x.

Exterior shells: thermal IR per 1 % 4.8 (1.02 AU), 2.7 (1.36), 1.25 (2), 0.56 (3), 0.20 (5), 0.05 (10 AU) ~ 1/r^2. Specular retro-reflection from an exterior shell converges back on Earth ((1-alpha) f S0 at any r: +0.95 W/m2 per 1 %), so exterior films need diffuse or absorbed NIR.

Front-face emissivity is the strongest lever for any population whose fronts face Earth: tuning eps_f to 0.37 (film at the 85 C design point at 1 AU) cuts co-orbital IR 40 %; a directional front (eps 0.15 within 50 deg of the normal) cuts it 76 %.

architectures.name: e_L1_thermostat
architectures.geometry: Cloud of ordinary compute sails near the beta = 0.004 L1 point (1.568e6 km sunward of Earth; 1.498e6 km for beta = 0), radius ~1 R_E around the Sun-Earth line, removing a fraction s of the sunlight that reaches Earth.
architectures.forcing_W_m2: -238 s (absorbed sunlight removed); its own IR reaches Earth at (R_E/d)^2 = 1.65e-5 of what it blocks
architectures.shade_fraction_needed: s = net_IR / 238 = 0.42 % of sunlight per W/m2 to cancel
architectures.can_be_compute_sails: Yes. A 279 m sail at L1 is an ordinary 349 K sail at 0.99 AU; a 1 % shade is 2.4e12 m2 (3.5e7 sails, 4e11 kg, ~6e14 W of chips): 1e-10 of a 10 % swarm. Its back faces point at Earth but Earth fills only 1.65e-5 of their hemisphere.
architectures.sunlight_loss: s (by design); the far-side swarm itself removes none
architectures.max_coverage: not a compute architecture; sized to the swarm
architectures.stationkeeping: L1 e-folding 24.505 days (beta 0.004); a sail displaced dx along the unstable direction needs ~lambda^2 dx = 2.2e-6 m/s2 per 10,000 km, so a cloud 1 R_E wide and +-1e4 km long fits the 3e-5 m/s2 authority, while Angel-type +-5e4 km clouds use most of it: use forced Lissajous/halo-type orbits (Sanchez & McInnes 2015) or thinner thermostat sails (beta ~0.01).
architectures.stability: Unstable (24-day e-folding); a dead shade sail leaves within months, so the shade fails safe (sunlight returns), and the swarm itself can be throttled by tilting (IR down within hours) - no termination shock if attitude control survives.
architectures.notes: The thermostat converts a global-mean warming into a sunlight-for-IR substitution; it is cheap in mass (1e-10 of the swarm) but not free in climate: side effects scale with the IR it cancels (see climate_side_effects_per_Wm2_cancelled).
regional_seasonal_notes: Pattern: the swarm IR (absorbed at 0.95 everywhere) replaces sunlight that would have been absorbed at 1 - albedo; bright regions (ice sheets, sea ice, snow, cloud decks) gain net heat, dark oceans and forests lose it. With a far-side swarm the IR arrives from within 45 deg of the Sun, so the diurnal and seasonal timing matches sunlight (5.5 % at night).

Per W/m2 cancelled: poles 60-90 +0.23 W/m2 annual (+0.41 in polar summer, +0.95 over a 0.8-albedo ice surface in June), tropics -0.16 W/m2; a diffusive EBM gives +0.04-0.07 K polar, -0.02 K tropical (no ice-albedo feedback; real polar amplification larger).

Vertical: 92 % of the swarm IR is absorbed in the atmosphere (only the clear-sky 8-12 um window reaches the surface, ~8 %), while the shade removes sunlight that was 67 % surface-absorbed: the surface loses ~0.59 W/m2 per W/m2 cancelled, the atmosphere gains it. Fast response: global precipitation -0.76 % per W/m2 (Andrews et al. 2010 energetics; cf. GeoMIP G1 -4.5 %, Tilmes et al. 2013).
Stratosphere warms ~0.27 K per W/m2 (CO2 15 um core absorbed above ~20 km) - the opposite sign to CO2 forcing.

Exterior swarms are worst for pattern: their IR is isotropic (50 % at night, same at all latitudes and seasons) while the shade removes daytime, low-latitude sunlight: polar residual +0.60, tropics -0.35 W/m2 per W/m2.

Cloud shape at L1 can tailor the dimming across Earth's disk (a cloud of radius 1 R_E dims the limb to ~0.53 of the sub-solar point; 2 R_E dims uniformly at 25 % efficiency): partially counter the polar residual by shading high latitudes (Sanchez & McInnes 2015).
literature: Angel 2006 PNAS: 1.8 % reduction, ~20 Mt cloud of 1-g flyers, 100,000 km long, 25 yr
Govindasamy & Caldeira 2000: ~1.8 % solar reduction offsets 2xCO2 with small regional residuals
Kravitz et al. 2013 (GeoMIP G1, 4xCO2 offset by 3.2-5 % solar reduction): tropics -0.3 K, poles +0.8 K
Tilmes et al. 2013: G1 global precipitation -4.5 %, monsoon land -5 to -7 %
Bala et al. 2008: hydrological cycle more sensitive to solar than to CO2 forcing
Sanchez & McInnes 2015: two-disk L1 configurations reduce latitudinal/seasonal residuals

phasing.note: keep-out phasing: conjunction must fall within +-45 deg of the orbit's highest/lowest point: up to 90 deg of phase per synodic period

interior_shell_0p91.note: Time-mean dimming of Earth = coverage on its sun-line = f for a uniform shell. Corridor = band of the shell that Earth's penumbral cone sweeps in a year: 2 sin(w) of the sphere / 2 = sin(w).

shadow.rings_note: A polar ring is seen from the Sun as a great-circle band; Earth crosses it twice a year and is dimmed by the band optical depth tau = f / sin(half-width) for 2 x half-width / 0.986 days. An ecliptic ring dims Earth permanently by tau. Rings concentrate shadow in time or space.
shadow.coorbital: Far-side sails (|lon - L3| <= 90 deg) are never between the Sun and Earth: zero transits, zero dimming.
shadow.exterior: Exterior sails never lie between the Sun and Earth (Earth is inside the shell): zero dimming.
shadow.summary: One 279 m sail casts a 27 km umbra at 0.91 AU (98x its size); at Earth (0.09 AU away) its penumbral spot is 68,800 km in radius (10.8 R_E) and only 4.7e-12 deep, so shading is purely collective. A uniform 0.91 AU shell dims Earth by exactly f on average; each sail transits once per 6.6-yr synodic period with probability 5.5e-4 (Monte Carlo 5.6e-4), lasting 1.4 h median (10 h for i = 0, 2.7 h for i = 30 deg); 2.1e9 sails shade Earth at once at f = 1 %, so flicker is ~2e-7 of sunlight. A shadow-free corridor costs 0.055 % of the shell and ~1 m/s per synodic period, but it removes the self-dimming that offsets 57-62 % of the IR. Rings concentrate shadow: a polar ring of +-1 deg at f = 1 % dims Earth 57 % for 2 days twice a year; an ecliptic ring dims it permanently. Far-side co-orbital and exterior swarms never transit. L1 thermostat: penumbral spot 7,370 km (1.16 R_E); a cloud of radius <= 1 R_E puts 53-74 % of what it blocks on Earth.

rules.note: Flakes keep the film beta (~0.004, 0.002 tumbling) and stay in the swarm orbit; only grains below ~5 um (beta > 0.04) released at 0.91 AU reach Earth's orbit; below ~0.4 um they leave the Solar System.

findings: Fragments of the film keep the film's areal density, so beta stays 0.004 (0.002 tumbling): flakes stay in the swarm's orbits. Only grains below ~5 um (beta > 0.04) released at 0.91 AU reach Earth's orbit (aphelion r0/(1-2 beta)); below ~0.4 um they are blown out.

Earth sweeps up an unbound grain with probability (R_E/2 AU)^2 = 4.5e-10; a bound Earth-crossing grain with ~1e-6 (f = 1 %) to 4e-8 (f = 22 %): the swarm itself removes Earth-crossing dust within ~1/f orbits (each perihelion crosses the sail layer).

Loss stream: with ~3e19 kg/yr unrecycled at the ceiling, keeping Earth's dust influx within 10 % of the natural 4e7 kg/yr needs fine (< 5 um) dust production below ~4e12 kg/yr (f = 1 %) to 1e14 kg/yr (f = 22 %), i.e. < 1e-7-3e-6 of the loss stream. Retired film must be recycled or returned as coarse slag, never ground, ablated or shattered in orbit.

Meteoroid erosion: the Gruen flux would put 8e13 kg/yr (f = 1 %) of meteoroids into the sails, but that would sweep the inner zodiacal cloud (~6e14 kg) in ~8 yr; in steady state impacts are limited by the cloud supply (1e3-1e4 kg/s), giving 3e11-3e13 kg/yr of ejecta (yield 10-100) and an Earth influx of 0.7-70 % (f = 1 %) or 0.03-3 % (f = 22 %) of natural. The swarm is a net dust sink.
Zodiacal light: the swarm's own cross-section at f = 1 % (2.6e21 m2) is ~1e4x the whole zodiacal cloud (1.7-3.5e17 m2), so dust brightening is negligible next to the swarm itself (see sky).

Derelicts: interior sails at 0.85-0.91 AU stay within +-0.008 AU for 1000 yr (N-body); at 0.95 AU low-inclination orbits are scattered by Earth to 0.89-0.99 AU, so the shell must stay below ~0.92 AU. Far-side co-orbital sails are in Earth's orbit by design: uncontrolled live sails librate to 0.29 AU (13 deg) of Earth; tumbling derelicts (beta 0.002) to 0.21 AU; dense debris (beta 0) passes within 0.035-0.05 AU dozens of times in 3 kyr (none inside the Hill sphere). Upper bound for dense debris that leaves the horseshoe zone: ~7e-8 impacts per object per year - dense parts (hubs, booms, pods, slag) must be tugged out of 1 AU.
Whole sails that do enter (0.2 kg/m2) ablate above ~120 km: a meteoric-smoke source, not an impactor. Satellites in Earth orbit see the same relative change as the influx (keep < 10 %).

findings: Every architecture lights Earth's sky long before it threatens the climate. At the 1 W/m2 limits the sky is 1e3-1e5x the natural night-sky luminance (1.7e-4 cd/m2, 22 mag/arcsec2) wherever the swarm is above the horizon.

Interior shell: a uniform glow of 1.45 cd/m2 per 1 % (12.2 mag/arcsec2 at 1 %) out to 62-65 deg from the Sun; after astronomical twilight the ground still gets 0.58 lux per 1 % (2.3x full moon) until the Sun is 60 deg down. At the 22 % ceiling: 25 cd/m2, 10 lux.

Far-side co-orbital: the glow is confined within 41-45 deg of the Sun: 4.8 cd/m2 per 1 % within 10 deg, 1.7 at 30-45 deg; ground 0.31 lux per 1 % at astronomical twilight, 0 once the Sun is > 45 deg below the horizon. At high latitudes in summer the Sun never gets that low: an all-night glow.
Exterior: uniform over the whole sky all night: 0.04-0.18 cd/m2 at the fleet-limited coverage (14.5-16 mag/arcsec2, 0.1-0.55 lux).

To keep post-twilight ground light below full moon (0.25 lux at a 18 deg solar depression): co-orbital f <= 0.8 % at rho_v 0.003, 2.4 % at rho_v 0.001; interior shell f <= 0.43 %. A blacker front (rho_v <= 0.001) is the main lever.

Individual glints are 9th (0.09 AU) to 16th (2 AU) magnitude. Collectively, specular Al vanes would outshine the film near the retro-direction - for far-side sails that is toward Earth: vanes must be matte or switchable-reflectance (IKAROS RCD-type).

recommendation.architecture: Far-side co-orbital compute cloud with low-e fronts, plus an L1 thermostat. Sails share Earth's orbit (a = (1-beta)^(1/3) = 0.9987 AU, period 1 yr) and are parked at heliocentric longitudes 90-174 deg and 186-270 deg from Earth (L3 +-90 deg minus a +-6 deg keep-out) on orbits with i <= 30 deg, so they are never between the Sun and Earth and never closer than 1.41 AU. Every far-side sail sees Earth in its sunward hemisphere and never in its anti-sun one, so the front face is made IR-dark (transparent-conductive low-e coating, eps_f 0.05-0.10) and the back face (eps 0.93) sheds 90-95 % of the heat away from Earth; at 1 AU this runs the film at 370-375 K, i.e. chiplets at 105-110 C (b4/b5; energy per op x1.12-1.15 for 2100+ logic). Conservative variant b2: eps_f 0.37 at the 85 C design point. A front-side specular sub-bandgap filter retro-reflects the 20 % NIR toward the Sun; vanes are matte. Longitude is held with ~1e-8 m/s2 (~0.4 m/s/yr, 1/2500 of the radiation-force authority). A small cloud of ordinary sails near L1 (1.57e6 km) removes 0.42 % of sunlight per W/m2 of swarm IR so the global net forcing is ~0; the swarm can also be throttled by tilting if the shade fails. The interior 0.85-0.92 AU shell is retired as the default: per unit coverage it heats Earth as much and trades 3.9 W/m2 of sunlight for IR per 1 %.
why: Far side: no shadow, no transits, no sunlight-for-IR trade from the swarm itself, and 2.7x (film as designed), 4.6x (b2), 13x (b4) or 25x (b5) less gross IR per coverage than the shell.

Co-orbital is the only placement that keeps a fixed geometry relative to Earth with a 0.004-beta sail; everything at r != 1 AU sweeps past Earth every synodic period, and interior/exterior sails show Earth their back or front faces in turn.

Running chiplets 20-25 K hotter costs 16-19 % of FLOP per joule but cuts IR toward Earth 3-6x: under a forcing cap it is worth 2.5-4.6x more compute than the 85 C film (hot_power: 105-125 C is within +-4 % of FLOP/s per kg for 2100+ logic).

Hot (0.3-0.7 AU) and exterior (2-10 AU) placements lose: hot halves net forcing per coverage but loses 29-72 % of FLOP per joule; exterior cuts IR as 1/r^2 but needs r^2 more area, so the mass-limited swarm at 3/5/10 AU reaches only 2.1/0.77/0.19 % coverage (12/4.5/1.1 % of the ceiling compute) and lights the whole night sky.
recommendation.coverage_limits_rule: X is the added global-mean forcing. Passive = no thermostat: net <= X. With the thermostat the net is ~0 and the limit is set by the cancelled gross IR, capped at 2.5 X: a net X warms ~0.8X K and raises precipitation ~2X %, a cancelled gross G leaves ~0 K but cuts precipitation ~0.76 G % and adds +0.23 G W/m2 at the poles, so G = 2.5 X is the hydrologically equivalent load.

compute_vs_unconstrained.at_4_Wm2_note: At 4 W/m2 the fleet mass (18.7 % coverage at 1 AU) binds before the forcing for b3-b5; a front tuned between b2 and b4 (eps ~0.2, ~95 C) then maximises compute at ~70-80 % of the ceiling (b4 71 %, b3 83 %).

sky_limited.rule: ground illuminance <= full moon (0.25 lux) at a 18 deg solar depression, ecliptic vertical

compute_vs_unconstrained.sky_limit_note: Keeping post-twilight skylight under full-moon level would cap the far-side cloud at ~0.8 % (rho_v 0.003) to 2.4 % (rho_v 0.001) - tighter than the 1 W/m2 climate cap for b4/b5. Visible light, not heat, may be the binding Earth constraint.

open_questions: Front-face emissivity engineering: a visible-transparent low-e front (eps 0.05-0.10, TCO or thin-metal/dielectric stack) is mature in kind (low-e glass) but untested on 30 um c-Si film at 370 K, and its free-carrier absorption costs some PV current; a broadband, unpolarised directional emitter (b3) has only been shown p-polarised over 8-14 um.

Chiplets at 105-110 C (b4/b5): SRAM leakage (already 10-59 % of a 0.15 W chiplet at 85 C) and NVM retention at 110 C must be checked; the 2100+ energy slope (x1.12-1.15) is from the hot-logic study, not a demonstration.

Specular vs diffuse sub-bandgap reflection: a textured cell with a back reflector scatters NIR diffusely (+0.5 W/m2 per 1 % for the co-orbital cloud); a front multilayer is specular. Which stack keeps alpha 0.80 and light trapping?

Thermostat climate response: the residual (polar summer +0.4 W/m2 per W/m2, precipitation -0.76 %/W/m2, stratosphere +0.27 K/W/m2) comes from an EBM and a band-partition estimate; it needs a GCM experiment with a 330-350 K diluted source near the Sun.
The 2.5x rule that maps cancelled IR to an equivalent net forcing is a hydrological argument; with ice-albedo feedback the polar residual may bind first.
Collision-free choreography of ~1e17-1e18 co-orbital sails on i <= 30 deg orbits (relative speeds up to ~15 km/s at nodes) and shading losses inside the cloud (assumed tau <= 0.9).
Night-sky light: is 0.3-1 lux of post-twilight glow within 45 deg of the Sun acceptable? It may bind before 1 W/m2 unless rho_v <= 0.001.
Dense co-orbital debris: long-term (Myr) impact probability of beta = 0 fragments that leave the horseshoe zone, and a retrieval rate requirement; the CR3BP/N-body runs cover only 1-3 kyr.
Exterior concentrators (thin Al mirrors feeding edge-on radiators at 3-5 AU) could escape the r^2 mass penalty and the 1/r^2 IR law at once, but would light the whole night sky; not quantified here.
L1 thermostat station-keeping with beta 0.004 uses most of the control authority; thinner (beta ~0.01) thermostat sails or forced Lissajous orbits are needed.
